newsitem.title: USA: NHL ICE HOCKEY-AVALANCHE-RED WINGS SET TO RESUME BITTER RIVALRY.
newsitem.headline: NHL ICE HOCKEY-AVALANCHE-RED WINGS SET TO RESUME BITTER RIVALRY.

text.p: There is no love lost between the Colorado Avalanche and Detroit Red Wings -- only blood.
The defending Stanley Cup champion Avalanche and the Red Wings resume their bitter rivalry when the National Hockey League's Western Conference finals begin Thursday.

The last meeting between these clubs in March resembled the notorious 1956 Soviet Union v Hungary Olympic water polo match, except it was easier to see the blood on the ice. The blood-letting in that 6-5 overtime win by Detroit was produced by 11 separate skirmishes, including one between the goalies.

The league has warned both teams it will not tolerate a repeat of that kind of display, which forced officials to stop the game to scrape blood off the ice. But hockey players in the heat of battle have been known to ignore league officials.
"This should be fun," said feisty Avalanche right wing Mike Keane. "You want to play against teams you don't like."
The focal point of the acrimony is Colorado's Claude Lemieux, the only player in the NHL more annoying to opponents than the New York Rangers' Esa Tikkanen.

Lemieux, a key player for three different Stanley Cup winners -- Montreal, New Jersey and Colorado -- is on his usual post-season roll, which means scoring more goals in the playoffs than during all of the regular season.

He leads the league with 10, but a knack for scoring big goals is often overshadowed by his reputation as one of the league's less gentlemanly players. "I don't hate anyone but the playoffs are my time," he said.

In last year's conference finals, won by Colorado in six games, Lemieux checked Detroit's Kris Draper head first into the boards with such force that Draper suffered a broken jaw and a number of other broken facial bones.
The gruesome sight of Draper, his face reminiscent of fresh hamburger meat, is one Detroit has not forgotten.

Potential fisticuffs aside, these teams bring a tremendous amount of talent to the table and exciting end-to-end hockey should thrill fans tired of the boring neutral zone trap game in vogue with many NHL teams these days.

Colorado, led by two of the game's brighest stars in Joe Sakic (4 goals, 15 assists) and gifted Swede Peter Forsberg (5g, 11a), won the President's Trophy for the best record in the NHL (49-24-9, 107 points) and they now know what it takes to win a Stanley Cup.

They also have enough depth -- with the likes of Valeri Kamenski (8 goals), Adam Deadmarsh and defenceman of the year candidate Sandis Ozolinsh -- that when Sakic and Forsberg both went down with extended mid-season injuries, the Avalanche rolled along without missing a beat.
Adding to Colorado's comfort zone is Patrick Roy, the best big-game goalie in the business with three Stanley Cups under his belt and the all-time NHL record for playoff wins (94).
The hungry Red Wings have more important things than revenge on their minds, carrying the weight of a 42-year title drought on their shoulders.

Despite being one of the league's elite clubs for most of the decade, the Wings have failed to make the breakthrough, losing in the finals as heavy favourites in 1995 and falling to Colorado at this stage last year.

Steve Yzerman, who has endured the last 14 years of the drought -- usually as Detroit's best player -- made his frustration clear last year and is ready to lay it all on the line for a sip of champagne from Lord Stanley's Cup.
This year his teammates seem to be showing some of the heart their captain has long displayed.

After an uneven six-game series against St Louis, Detroit swept Anaheim in four, rising to the occasion in three nerve-wracking sudden death situations, with one game going to triple overtime and the clincher ending in double OT.

Mike Vernon has been tremendous for Detroit in goal with a 1.80 goals against average and takes tremendous confidence from coming out on the winning end of three pressure-packed overtime contests in the last four games.

And after much tinkering with his lines and even trying superb two-way forward Sergei Fedorov on defence, legendary Red Wings coach Scotty Bowman reunited his "Russian unit" in the playoffs and it has paid off handsomely.

The quintet of Fedorov, Vyacheslav Kozlov, Igor Larionov, Slava Fetisov and Vladimir Konstantinov -- the last three veterans of legendary Soviet teams of the 1980s -- have been creating scoring chances and producing big goals for Detroit.
But to advance to the championship round, the Red Wings must win at least one game in Denver with Colorado holding home ice advantage -- and that is no small task.
Colorado, which needed six games to take out Chicago and five to finish off Edmonton, have been unbeatable at home in the playoffs -- going 7-0 and outscoring their opponents 38-9.
"We understand how we have to play to beat Colorado," Bowman said.
"It's discipline and defence -- plus Vernon has to play at least even with Roy."
Easier said than done.
